title: The Roots of Working-Class Men's Discontent | Institute for Family Studies
gist: Using the Global Flourishing Study (200,000+ respondents, 22 countries; 18,178 U.S. men aged 25+), this IFS brief argues that childhood family conditions — above all the father-son relationship — explain 18%-33% of the well-being gap between working-class and college-educated American men. It pairs this with hard trend data: marriage among working-class men ages 25-44 fell from 73% in 1980 to 42% in 2025, and the white non-Hispanic male suicide rate ages 25-44 rose from 31 to 54 per 100,000 between 1992 and 2023.

insights.claim: The share of American men ages 25 to 44 who report being 'not too happy' in the General Social Survey has risen from 11% in the 1980s to 24% in the most recent years.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A doubling of self-reported male unhappiness over four decades is a structural demand signal for everything from gambling and gaming to pharmaceuticals and populist politics.

insights.claim: The unhappiness gap is class-stratified: 27% of men without a bachelor's degree report being 'not too happy' versus 17% of college-educated men.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Educational attainment is the cleanest available proxy for male well-being divergence — a segmentation variable for consumer and political models.

insights.claim: The suicide rate per 100,000 white non-Hispanic men ages 25 to 44 rose from 31 in 1992 to 54 in 2023, a 71% increase over three decades, concentrated among the white working class.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Deaths of despair are still accelerating, not plateauing — a hard mortality signal underpinning the labour-supply and disability-claims trend.

insights.claim: The class gap in male happiness is not new — GSS data show college-educated men were happier than less-educated peers as far back as the 1980s — so the story is widening, not novel, disparity.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Guards against treating the male malaise as a recent, reversible shock; it is a four-decade trend with compounding effects.
insights.locator: The class disparity in happiness is nothing new.

themes.theme: Family Collapse as the Missing Variable

insights.claim: Economists blame the economy, journalists blame ideologies among the less educated, and influencers blame a crisis of masculinity — but the authors argue the factor hidden in plain sight in explanations of working-class male discontent is the family.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reframes the male malaise debate away from wages and culture-war explanations toward a measurable, intergenerational household variable.
insights.quote: But woefully missing from this conversation is a factor hidden in plain sight: the family.
insights.locator: Experts from all leanings have provided explanations

insights.claim: The share of working-class men ages 25 to 44 who are married fell from 73% in 1980 to 42% in 2025, according to the Current Population Survey.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A 31-point collapse in marriage among prime-age non-college men reshapes household formation, single-occupancy housing demand and consumption patterns.

themes.theme: The Father-Son Relationship as Primary Mechanism

insights.claim: Compared to college-educated men, working-class men are 17 percentage points less likely to have grown up with married parents, 11 points less likely to have had a good relationship with their father, and 10 points less likely to have felt loved by their father.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Quantifies the childhood-input gap that precedes and predicts the adult well-being gap — the disadvantage is inherited, not just earned.

insights.claim: Childhood family variables jointly explain between 18% and 33% of the well-being gap between college-educated and working-class men ages 25-44 in a coefficient attenuation framework.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Sizes the family channel: material but far from total, so family policy alone cannot close the male well-being gap.

insights.claim: Across all models, the relationship with the father is the single most significant explanatory variable linking class to well-being, alone explaining nearly one-third of the difference in hope between college-educated and working-class young men.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Isolates father involvement — not household income or maternal relationship — as the highest-leverage intervention point for male outcomes.

insights.claim: Hope is the well-being outcome most explained by childhood family conditions, while sense of life being worthwhile and sense of purpose are explained less by family variables.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Differentiates which psychological deficits are family-transmitted versus economically or socially produced — relevant to targeting interventions.

insights.claim: The authors argue the psychological foundations of a hopeful and meaningful life are transmitted — or fail to be transmitted — through the family of origin, with the father relationship as the primary channel.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A transmission-mechanism model implying that today's family instability produces a predictable well-being deficit one generation out.

insights.claim: On a 10-point scale, working-class men score .21 lower on hope, .52 lower on life being worthwhile, and .44 lower on purpose than college-educated men — small-to-moderate effects with Cohen's d ranging from .10 to .28.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The headline class gap is statistically real but modest; the authors themselves caution against overstating the plight of working-class men as a whole.

insights.claim: The class gap in well-being is pronounced among young men but essentially disappears among men ages 45 and older, where working-class and college-educated men report similar scores.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The crisis is age-concentrated, so it may reflect a life-stage effect that partly self-corrects — a check on the most alarmist readings.

insights.claim: The analysis draws on the first wave of the Global Flourishing Study, a 2023 multinational survey of over 200,000 participants across 22 countries, restricted here to 18,178 U.S. male respondents aged 25 and older.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A large, newly available dataset that will generate follow-on findings — worth tracking as a recurring source of family and well-being signal.
